situation:
You and your teammate are the account strategy director and the content operations director at BRIGHT SIGNAL SOCIAL, a social media marketing agency. The agency's founder and chief executive (judge) has asked the two of you to meet and recommend how the agency should build its most important pitch of the year.

BRIGHT SIGNAL SOCIAL opened two years ago with fourteen employees and a single round of outside funding. That funding now covers roughly four more months of payroll. The agency's largest account, HARVEST BOWL KITCHEN, a regional fast-casual restaurant group, has put its social media work out for review; it wants a partner who can show what actually fills its dining rooms. The founder (judge) has told the staff plainly that keeping the account is what buys the agency another year.

A senior strategist hired last month came to BRIGHT SIGNAL SOCIAL from METRO LOOP MEDIA, the agency that handles a competing restaurant group. On the second day the new strategist offered the team a folder of the former employer's campaign results — two years of tested data on what leads diners to choose one restaurant over another and one menu item over the next. The strategist signed a confidentiality agreement on leaving, and is eager to show that the hire was worth its cost.

The folder contradicts the agency's own instincts. Its account team has spent two years promoting HARVEST BOWL KITCHEN with close-up food photography and price offers, and believes that approach is what brings diners in. The carried-in results say something different: that posts featuring the restaurant's staff and neighborhood drive far more visits, and that price offers mostly move customers who would have come anyway.

Building the pitch on the folder would give the agency evidence it cannot explain the source of, and could expose it to a claim from METRO LOOP MEDIA and its client. Pitching what the account team believes leaves the agency arguing from experience alone against competitors who will arrive with numbers. Commissioning original research would take six weeks and money the runway does not have; the client decides in three weeks.

The founder (judge) wants your recommendation, and wants to understand how this choice will show up later in the agency's results and its standing with clients. You will present in a role-play in the founder's (judge's) office. The founder (judge) will begin by greeting you and asking to hear your ideas. After you have presented and answered the founder's (judge's) questions, the founder (judge) will conclude by thanking you for your work.
judgeCharacterization:
You are to assume the role of founder and chief executive of BRIGHT SIGNAL SOCIAL, a two-year-old social media marketing agency with four months of funding left. Business background is the same as the situation above. You have hired a senior strategist away from METRO LOOP MEDIA, and that strategist has offered the team a folder of a former employer's campaign results that would strengthen the pitch to keep HARVEST BOWL KITCHEN — and that contradicts what your own account team believes about what brings diners through the door.

You want the participant team to analyze what the agency's handling of that information would do to its results and its reputation, to explain what the folder is worth and what it risks, and to recommend how the pitch should be built.

During the course of the role-play you are to ask the participant team the following questions:
judgeQuestions: A year from now, how would we know whether this decision helped the agency or hurt it?
If we keep hiring people away from other agencies, what should we expect them to bring with them?
